blocks.text: A fourth interpretation is found in the Arabic paraphrase of Isaiah, where for the Hebrew ינשוף jansuph and the Greek ἴβις [ibis] one reads الحباري [al-ḥubārā] alhubara. Gabriel Sionita wrongly renders this as "eagle owls", since حباري [ḥubārā] hubara is the otis [bustard], or tarda, if you prefer ^{(4)}. So the translators of Avicenna render it in book 2, in the chapter On eggs; nor had they rendered it otherwise in the chapter On dung, although the ignorance of scribes changed tardam into turdum [thrush]. So also Andreas Bellunensis in his Explanation of the Arabic names of Avicenna; and the lexicographers too, such as Giggeius, Golius, etc. That this explanation is correct is shown by the description of the bird in Abenbitar, taken from Assariph: هو طاير كبير العنق رمادي اللون في منقاره بعض الطول وهو مشهور لحمه بين لحم الدجاج ولحم البط وهو اخف من لحم البط لانه بري وفيه شي [col. 283] من الغلظ [huwa ṭāyir kabīr al-ʿunuq ramādī al-lawn fī minqārihi baʿḍ al-ṭūl wa-huwa mashhūr laḥmuhu bayna laḥm al-dajāj wa-laḥm al-baṭṭ wa-huwa akhaff min laḥm al-baṭṭ li-annahu barrī wa-fīhi shī min al-ghilaẓ] "It is a bird with a large neck, of ashen colour, with a somewhat long beak, very well known (that is, in the East); its flesh is midway between that of the hen and that of the goose, but lighter than goose, because it is a land bird, although it has something coarse about it" ^{(5)}. [III, 27] Damir adds: وسلاحها سلاحها [wa-silāḥuhā silāḥuhā] "And its dung serves it as a weapon", playing on the ambiguity of the word سلاح [silāḥ], which means both "dung" and "weapon". Alkazuinius explains the matter thus: اذا تصدها الصقر لا يزل يعلوا وينزل مع الصقر حتي تجد قصد فرماه بدرقه يبقا الصقر مقيدا مثل المكتوف فعند ذلك يجتمع الحباريات وينتف ريشه وفي ذلك هلاك الصقر [idhā taṣaddahā al-ṣaqr lā yazal yaʿlū wa-yanzil maʿa al-ṣaqr ḥattā tajid qaṣd fa-ramāhu bi-darqihi yabqā al-ṣaqr muqayyadan mithl al-maktūf fa-ʿinda dhālika yajtamiʿ al-ḥubāriyyāt wa-yantif rīshahu wa-fī dhālika halāk al-ṣaqr] "When the hawk pursues it, it does not cease to rise and descend with the hawk until, hitting its eye, it has cast its dung into it. When this is done, the hawk remains bound, like one tied hand and foot. Then the bustards gather and pluck the hawk's feathers, whence certain death for it" ^{(6)}. Alluding to this, a poet says the following of someone who had befouled himself out of fear while fleeing:
وهم تركوه اسلح من حباري ✡ راي صقرا واشرد من نعام ✡ [wa-hum tarakūhu aslaḥ min ḥubārā ✡ raʾā ṣaqran wa-ashrad min naʿām ✡]

"And they left him more beshitten than a bustard that has seen a hawk, and more given to flight than an ostrich." They say too that it is most melancholy and is consumed with grief when its feathers grow back slowly after moulting; and that from this arose the common proverb اكبد من الحباري [akbad min al-ḥubārā] "More melancholy than a bustard." It is added that it deserts its own eggs in order to brood those of others. But Damir clears it of this charge, as we have said elsewhere ^{a)}. Its eggs are used for blackening the hair, but only the male ones, that is, those from which males are to be hatched; these are distinguished by inserting a thread, for from a male egg it is drawn out black. In its crop lies a stone which stops a flux and prevents dreams. In Persian the bustard is called جرز [jurz] gerez; the male in Egyptian usage حبرج [ḥubruj] hubarig. The chick is called in Arabic نهار [nahār] nehar, as that of the partridge is ليل [layl] lail.
